The invitation was to sacrificial feasts (25:2), and a psalm speaks of eating "the sacrifices of the dead," which some scholars connect with funeral feasts. Sexual immorality and idolatry are bound together.

insights.title: Judgment on the leaders
insights.body: God orders that the chiefs of the people be publicly executed "before the sun" (25:4); the exact meaning of the Hebrew verb, impaling or exposing, is uncertain. Moses tells Israel's judges to kill those who had joined themselves to Baal Peor (25:5). The text presents this as judgment on open covenant betrayal, and it makes for sobering reading.

insights.title: Qin'ah: jealousy and zeal
insights.body: Phinehas "was jealous with my jealousy" (25:11). The Hebrew qin'ah means both jealousy and zeal, the same word used in the jealousy ritual of chapter 5. God's jealousy is the passion of a husband for a covenant partner, not petty envy.

insights.title: Credited for righteousness
insights.body: Psalm 106 says Phinehas's act "was credited to him for righteousness, for all generations," the same phrase used of Abraham's faith. Later Jewish rebels, from the Maccabees to the Zealots of Jesus' day, looked to Phinehas as their model of zeal.

insights.title: Twenty-four or twenty-three thousand?
insights.body: Numbers gives 24,000 dead in the plague (25:9). Paul, warning the Corinthians, says "in one day twenty-three thousand fell." Explanations include Paul counting only those who died on a single day, a difference in what is counted, or a slip of memory; the point is the same.

insights.title: A covenant of peace
insights.body: God gives Phinehas "my covenant of peace" and an everlasting priesthood (25:12-13). The high priestly line ran through Phinehas to Zadok, the chief priest in Solomon's day. Malachi recalls God's covenant with Levi as one "of life and peace."

insights.title: Zeal and violence
insights.body: Scripture praises Phinehas, yet later movements used his example to justify violence of their own choosing, and Jesus rebuked his disciples for wanting fire from heaven. How can you tell zeal for God from zeal for your own cause?

26.summary: After the plague, Moses and Eleazar count the new generation on the plains of Moab, clan by clan, as the basis for dividing the land; none of the men counted at Sinai remains except Caleb and Joshua.
26.lookfor: Compare each tribe's total with chapter 1, notice the asides about Korah, Er and Onan and the daughters named in the list, and read the closing verses closely.

names.name: Eleazar
names.gloss: Aaron's son, now high priest, who leads the census with Moses.

names.name: Zelophehad
names.gloss: A man of Manasseh who died leaving five daughters and no sons.

names.name: Serah
names.gloss: A daughter of Asher, Jacob's son, unusually named in a list of men.

names.name: Jochebed
names.gloss: Mother of Moses, Aaron and Miriam.

names.name: Perez
names.gloss: Son of Judah and Tamar, ancestor of David.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: Grandson of Manasseh, whose name is also given to a region east of the Jordan.

names.name: Korahites
names.gloss: Levites descended from Korah, whose line survived his rebellion.

skim.advice: Verses 5 to 50 list the clans of each tribe with their totals. Skim the names, but stop at the asides (verses 9 to 11, 19, 33 and 46) and read verses 52 to 65 closely.

insights.title: A new generation
insights.body: "There was not a man left of them, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun" (26:65). The sentence of chapter 14 has run its course. The scholar Dennis Olson argued that the two censuses frame the whole book: the death of the old generation in chapters 1 to 25 and the birth of the new in chapters 26 to 36.

insights.title: Totals compared
insights.body: The new total, 601,730 (26:51), is almost the same as the first. But individual tribes changed greatly: Simeon fell from 59,300 to 22,200 (26:14), while Manasseh rose from 32,200 to 52,700 (26:34). Some connect Simeon's loss with the plague at Peor, where Zimri, a Simeonite leader, was killed.

insights.title: Korah's sons survived
insights.body: The list pauses to recall Dathan and Abiram, then adds, "Notwithstanding, the sons of Korah didn't die" (26:11). Their descendants became Temple singers, and their name heads eleven psalms, including Psalm 84.

insights.title: Women in a list of men
insights.body: The census counts males, yet it names Zelophehad's five daughters (26:33), Serah the daughter of Asher (26:46), Jochebed and Miriam (26:59). The daughters of Zelophehad prepare for the next chapter. Later Jewish legend made Serah a long-lived keeper of family memory.

insights.title: From Perez to David
insights.body: Judah's clans include Perez and his son Hezron (26:20-21). Matthew's genealogy of Jesus runs through Perez, Hezron and Nahshon, the leader of Judah in chapter 1. The aside about Er and Onan (26:19) recalls the troubled family story behind Perez's birth.

insights.title: By size and by lot
insights.body: Larger tribes are to get more land (26:54), but the land is also divided "by lot" (26:55). The lot was trusted to express God's choice, as a proverb says: the lot is cast into the lap, "but its every decision is from Yahweh." Need and divine allotment work together.

insights.title: Moses' family in brief
insights.body: In the middle of the Levites comes Moses' own family: Jochebed, a daughter of Levi, bore Aaron, Moses and Miriam (26:59). Hebrews praises Moses' parents for hiding him by faith. The family that began Israel's rescue is listed among the dead and the living.

insights.title: Counted again
insights.body: Thirty-eight years after the first census, a whole new set of names fills the same tribes. What do you hope will be true of the generation after yours?

27.summary: The five daughters of Zelophehad ask for their father's land and God grants it, creating a new inheritance law; Moses is shown the land he will not enter, asks God for a successor, and commissions Joshua.
27.lookfor: Notice how the daughters make their case, God's verdict, Moses' request for the people rather than for himself, and how authority passes to Joshua.

names.name: Zelophehad
names.gloss: A man of Manasseh who died in the wilderness leaving five daughters.

names.name: Mahlah
names.gloss: The eldest-named of Zelophehad's daughters.

names.name: Noah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's daughters; in Hebrew a different name from Noah of the flood.

names.name: Hoglah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's daughters.

names.name: Milcah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's daughters.

names.name: Tirzah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's daughters; a town of the same name later became a royal city.

names.name: Abarim
names.gloss: The mountain range east of the Dead Sea that includes Mount Nebo.

insights.title: Not in Korah's company
insights.body: The daughters stress that their father was not part of Korah's rebellion; "he died in his own sin" (27:3), as one of the wilderness generation. Their question is about his name: "Why should the name of our father be taken away?" (27:4). Land kept a family's name alive in Israel.

insights.title: Standing at the door
insights.body: The five women come before Moses, Eleazar, the leaders and the whole congregation at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting (27:2). It is the most public place in Israel. Moses does not decide himself but brings "their cause before Yahweh" (27:5).

insights.title: The daughters speak right
insights.body: God's verdict is direct: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right" (27:7). Their case becomes a law for all Israel, setting an order of inheritance (27:8-11). Rabbinic tradition praised them as wise and learned, and Joshua records that they received their land.

insights.title: Seeing the land
insights.body: Moses is told to climb the Abarim range and see the land (27:12-14). Deuteronomy tells the scene in full: Moses goes up Mount Nebo, sees the land, and dies there. The reason given, the waters of Meribah, connects back to chapter 20.

insights.title: Sheep without a shepherd
insights.body: Moses' first thought is for the people: "that the congregation of Yahweh may not be as sheep which have no shepherd" (27:17). The prophet Micaiah uses the same image for a leaderless Israel, and the Gospels say Jesus had compassion on the crowds because they were like sheep without a shepherd.

insights.title: Hands on Joshua
insights.body: Moses lays his hand on Joshua, "a man in whom is the Spirit" (27:18), in front of the priest and the whole congregation (27:22-23). Deuteronomy adds that Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. The laying on of hands for commissioning continues in the early church.

insights.title: Urim: asking through the priest
insights.body: Joshua will not speak with God face to face as Moses did. He will stand before Eleazar, who will seek God's decision "by the judgment of the Urim" (27:21), sacred lots kept in the high priest's breastplate. Leadership after Moses is shared between the commander and the priest.

insights.title: Asking for others
insights.body: Told he is about to die, Moses asks not for himself but for a leader for the people. What would it look like to plan for those who come after you?

28.summary: God sets out the public offerings for Israel's calendar: two lambs every day, more on each Sabbath and new moon, and the offerings for the week of Passover and the Feast of Weeks.
28.lookfor: Notice how each special day adds to the daily offering instead of replacing it, the phrase 'my food', and the pattern of bulls, ram and lambs that keeps repeating.

skim.advice: The offerings are listed by occasion with the same amounts of flour, oil and wine each time. Read the daily offering (verses 2 to 8) closely, then skim for what each festival adds.

insights.title: A calendar for the new generation
insights.body: The new generation has been counted and a new leader appointed. Before a single battle west of the Jordan, God gives Israel a full calendar of public worship. Leviticus 23 tells the people when the festivals fall; these chapters tell the priests what must be offered on each one.

insights.title: The tamid
insights.body: Two year-old lambs are offered every day, one in the morning and one at evening (28:3-4), called "a continual burnt offering." The Hebrew is tamid, and a whole tractate of the Mishnah describes how it was carried out in the Temple. Daniel speaks of a time when the continual offering would be taken away.

insights.title: Lechem: my food
insights.body: God calls the offerings "my food" (28:2), Hebrew lachmi, from lechem, bread or food. Israel did not believe God needed feeding; a psalm has God ask whether he eats the meat of bulls. The language pictures a shared meal, with God as honoured guest at the centre of Israel's life.

insights.title: Always in addition
insights.body: Again and again the chapter says "besides the continual burnt offering" (28:10, 28:15, 28:23). The daily lambs never stop for a festival; special days are layered on top of ordinary faithfulness.

insights.title: Strong drink poured out
insights.body: The daily drink offering is "strong drink," Hebrew shekar (28:7), poured out in the holy place. It is a rare instance of shekar being given to God; elsewhere the drink offering is wine (28:14). Nothing is drunk; it is all poured out.

insights.title: The Feast of Weeks
insights.body: "The day of the first fruits" in the "feast of weeks" (28:26) came seven weeks after Passover. Greek-speaking Jews called it Pentecost, "fiftieth." On that day in Acts, the Spirit was poured out on the disciples, and Christians have read it as the first fruits of the church's harvest.

insights.title: Every day the same
insights.body: Hebrews contrasts the priests who stand "day by day" offering the same sacrifices with Christ's single offering for all time. The same letter urges a sacrifice of praise offered continually. The rhythm of the tamid becomes a rhythm of prayer.

insights.title: Morning and evening
insights.body: Israel's every day began and ended at the altar. A psalm asks that prayer rise like incense and lifted hands be like the evening sacrifice. How do you begin and end your days?

29.summary: The offerings for the seventh month: the day of trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the eight days of the Feast of Tabernacles, when the number of bulls drops by one each day from thirteen to seven.
29.lookfor: Watch the count of bulls through the feast, the smaller offering on the eighth day, and how the seventh month holds three festivals.

skim.advice: Verses 17 to 34 repeat the same formula for each day of the feast with one bull fewer each time. Skim them for the count, and read the opening festivals and the eighth day closely.

insights.title: The seventh month
insights.body: Just as the seventh day is the Sabbath, the seventh month is the high point of the year, holding three festivals: trumpets on the first day (29:1), atonement on the tenth (29:7) and Tabernacles from the fifteenth (29:12). The year's worship reaches its height in its own sabbath season.

insights.title: A day of blowing
insights.body: The first day of the seventh month is "a day of blowing of trumpets" (29:1), Yom Teruah. Jews keep it as Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, sounding the shofar. Numbers gives only its offerings; its meaning was developed in later Jewish tradition.

insights.title: The Day of Atonement
insights.body: On the tenth day Israel must "afflict your souls" (29:7), understood as fasting. The extra offerings here come "besides the sin offering of atonement" (29:11), the great rite described in Leviticus 16 with the two goats.

insights.title: Seventy bulls
insights.body: The bulls offered during the feast run 13, 12, 11, 10, 9, 8, 7 (29:13-32), seventy in all. The Talmud links the seventy bulls with the seventy nations listed in Genesis 10, saying Israel offered them on behalf of the world. Zechariah foresees the nations coming to keep this very feast.

insights.title: Counting down by sevens
insights.body: Every day of the feast also brings two rams and fourteen lambs. Across the seven days that makes 14 rams and 98 lambs, and the bulls end at seven on the seventh day (29:32). The whole festival is built from sevens.

insights.title: Atseret: the closing assembly
insights.body: The eighth day is "a solemn assembly" (29:35), Hebrew atseret, from a root meaning to hold back. After a week of abundance, the offering shrinks to one bull, one ram and seven lambs. Jewish tradition calls it Shemini Atzeret, and rabbis pictured God asking his people to stay one more day.

insights.title: The last and greatest day
insights.body: John sets one of Jesus' great sayings at this feast: "on the last and greatest day of the feast," Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him and drink. By then the Temple celebration included a daily procession pouring out water at the altar, described in the Mishnah.

insights.title: Abundance and a quiet ending
insights.body: The feast moves from thirteen bulls to one, and ends with a smaller, closer gathering. What would it look like to end a season of celebration by simply staying close to God?

30.summary: Moses explains how vows work: a man must keep his word, while a vow made by a daughter at home or by a wife can be cancelled by her father or husband on the day he hears it.
30.lookfor: Notice the different situations of a man, an unmarried daughter, a wife, and a widow or divorced woman, and the weight placed on 'the day that he hears'.

insights.title: Following the festivals
insights.body: The festival offerings end with a mention of "your vows" (Numbers 29:39), and this chapter follows on. Vows often promised an offering or a period of self-denial. The opening rule is simple: a man "shall not break his word" (30:2).

insights.title: Neder and issar
insights.body: The chapter uses two words: neder, a vow to give or do something, and issar, a "bond" by which someone binds themselves to abstain (30:2). Both bind the "soul," the whole person. Words spoken to God are treated as binding as a contract.

insights.title: Vows and the household
insights.body: A daughter's or wife's vow could commit household goods or affect family life, so the father or husband could annul it on the day he heard it (30:5, 30:8). The law reflects the household structure of its time. Yet a widow or divorced woman is fully responsible for her own vows (30:9), with no one able to cancel them.

insights.title: Silence is consent
insights.body: If the father or husband says nothing on the day he hears, the vow stands (30:4, 30:14). He cannot wait and cancel it later; if he does, "he shall bear her iniquity" (30:15). The woman is protected from a decision changed after the fact.

insights.title: Yahweh will forgive her
insights.body: Three times the chapter says that when a woman's vow is cancelled, "Yahweh will forgive her" (30:5, 30:8, 30:12). She is not counted guilty for a vow she was not allowed to keep. The law guards her conscience as well as the household's order.

insights.title: Hannah's vow
insights.body: Hannah vowed that if God gave her a son he would belong to Yahweh all his life. Her husband Elkanah, on hearing it, let it stand: "Do what seems good to you." Samuel's whole story rests on a wife's vow and a husband's consent.

insights.title: Let your yes be yes
insights.body: Ecclesiastes warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Jesus goes further, telling his followers not to swear at all: "let your 'Yes' be 'Yes' and your 'No' be 'No.'" Jephthah's rash vow in Judges shows how badly vows could go wrong.

insights.title: Words that bind
insights.body: This chapter treats spoken promises to God as seriously as legal contracts. Which promises have you made, to God or to others, that you need to remember?

31.summary: Israel wages war on Midian for the sin at Peor, killing its kings and Balaam; Moses orders the captive boys and the women who had been with men to be killed, and the plunder is purified and divided between soldiers, people and sanctuary.
31.lookfor: Notice the reason given for the war, Moses' anger at the officers and its reason, the purification rules, how the plunder is shared, and the officers' offering at the end.

names.name: Midianites
names.gloss: A desert people allied with Moab who drew Israel into the worship of Baal Peor.

names.name: Phinehas
names.gloss: Son of the high priest Eleazar, who goes with the army carrying the trumpets.

names.name: Balaam
names.gloss: The seer from chapters 22 to 24, now found among the Midianites.

names.name: Eleazar
names.gloss: The high priest, who gives the rules for purifying the soldiers and the plunder.

skim.advice: Verses 32 to 47 list the plunder and the shares in detail. Skim the figures, and read the reason for the war, Moses' order and the officers' gift closely.

insights.title: Vengeance for Peor
insights.body: God tells Moses to avenge Israel on the Midianites, "afterward you shall be gathered to your people" (31:2). It is Moses' last campaign. The war follows from God's earlier command after Peor, where Midian "harassed you with their wiles."

insights.title: Balaam's end
insights.body: Balaam is killed with the sword among the Midianites (31:8), and Moses says the women caused Israel to sin "through the counsel of Balaam" (31:16). The seer who once prayed, "Let me die the death of the righteous!" dies among Israel's enemies. Joshua remembers him simply as "the soothsayer."

insights.title: A deeply troubling chapter
insights.body: Moses orders the killing of the captive boys and of every woman who had been with a man, keeping the girls alive (31:17-18), presumably as wives or servants, under rules like those in Deuteronomy. The text presents it as judgment for Peor, but many readers, Jewish and Christian, find it among the hardest passages in Scripture. Some stress the conventions of ancient war writing, some a once-only judgment, and Christians read it alongside Jesus' command to love enemies; none of these makes it easy.

insights.title: Midian survives
insights.body: Although the chapter says every male was killed (31:7), Midian is strong enough a few generations later to oppress Israel for seven years in Gideon's day. Most scholars take the account to concern particular Midianite clans near Moab rather than the whole people.

insights.title: Through fire and water
insights.body: Metal that can survive fire must pass through fire, and everything else through water (31:22-23). Soldiers and captives stay outside the camp for seven days and are purified on the third and seventh days (31:19), applying the law of chapter 19 for contact with the dead.

insights.title: Sharing the spoil
insights.body: The plunder is split in half between the soldiers and the rest of the people (31:27), with a portion from each half for the priests and Levites. David later makes a similar rule that those who guard the baggage share equally with those who fight.

insights.title: Not one man missing
insights.body: The officers count their troops and report that "there lacks not one man of us" (31:49). They bring gold "to make atonement for our souls" (31:50). Exodus required a ransom when Israel was counted, and the officers may have had that in mind.

insights.title: Reading the hardest pages
insights.body: This chapter does not let readers look away from violence done in God's name. How do you read such a passage honestly while also listening to the rest of Scripture?

32.summary: Reuben and Gad ask to settle in the good grazing land east of the Jordan; Moses angrily compares them to the spies, and they agree to cross and fight with the other tribes before returning home.
32.lookfor: Notice what Moses fears the request will do to the rest of Israel, the deal that is struck, and the famous warning in the middle.

names.name: Reuben
names.gloss: The tribe descended from Jacob's firstborn, rich in livestock.

names.name: Gad
names.gloss: The tribe descended from Jacob's son Gad, also a tribe of herders.

names.name: Jazer
names.gloss: A town and region east of the Jordan with good pasture.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: The hilly, fertile region east of the Jordan, between the Yarmuk and the Arnon.

names.name: Machir
names.gloss: Son of Manasseh, whose clan takes Gilead.

names.name: Havvoth Jair
names.gloss: "The villages of Jair," a group of settlements in Gilead and Bashan.

names.name: Nobah
names.gloss: A man of Manasseh who captures Kenath and names it after himself.

insights.title: The spies all over again
insights.body: Moses hears the request, "Don't bring us over the Jordan" (32:5), and recalls Kadesh, when the spies discouraged the people (32:8-13). He fears the same refusal will doom the new generation. The whole story of Numbers 13 and 14 is retold in a few verses.

insights.title: Sheep first, children second
insights.body: The tribes offer to build "sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones" (32:16). Moses answers, "Build cities for your little ones, and folds for your sheep" (32:24), putting the children first. Rashi and other Jewish commentators noticed the gentle correction.

insights.title: Your sin will find you out
insights.body: "Be sure your sin will find you out" (32:23) became a proverb in English. In context it is quite specific: if Reuben and Gad break their promise to fight for their brothers, that failure is a sin against Yahweh that will catch up with them.

insights.title: Gad in the Mesha Stele
insights.body: The Moabite king Mesha's inscription of the 9th century BC says "the men of Gad" had lived in the land of Ataroth from of old, and boasts of taking Ataroth and Nebo from Israel. Both towns are named in this chapter (32:3, 32:34, 32:38). It is outside evidence that Gad lived where Numbers places it.

insights.title: The promise kept
insights.body: Joshua reminds the eastern tribes of their promise, and their fighting men cross the Jordan ahead of Israel. When they go home, they build an altar by the Jordan that nearly starts a civil war, until they explain it as a witness that they too belong to Yahweh.

insights.title: Living across the river
insights.body: Choosing land outside Canaan proper kept these tribes on the edge of Israel's life. Joshua 22 voices the worry that their land might be thought unclean. Centuries later they were among the first carried off by Assyria.

insights.title: Names changed
insights.body: The Reubenites rebuild Nebo and Baal Meon, "their names being changed" (32:38). Nebo is the name of a Babylonian god and Baal a Canaanite one, which may be why they were renamed. Jair names his villages Havvoth Jair (32:41), a name that lasts into the time of the judges.

insights.title: Shall you sit here?
insights.body: "Shall your brothers go to the war, and shall you sit here?" (32:6). Where might you be settling comfortably while others carry a burden you could share?

33.summary: Moses' record of Israel's journey from Rameses in Egypt to the plains of Moab, stage by stage, followed by God's command to drive out the inhabitants of Canaan and destroy their idols.
33.lookfor: Notice the familiar places from Exodus and Numbers, the long run of names found nowhere else, the note on Aaron's death, and the warning at the end.

names.name: Rameses
names.gloss: A store city in Egypt's Nile delta, where the exodus began.

names.name: Succoth
names.gloss: Israel's first camp after leaving Rameses.

names.name: Elim
names.gloss: An oasis with twelve springs and seventy palm trees.

names.name: Rephidim
names.gloss: The camp where water came from the rock and Israel fought Amalek.

names.name: Ezion Geber
names.gloss: A site at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, later Solomon's port.

names.name: Mount Hor
names.gloss: The mountain on the edge of Edom where Aaron died.

skim.advice: The list of camps (verses 5 to 49) uses one formula throughout. Skim the names, pausing at the places you know and at the notes in verses 8 to 9, 14 and 38 to 40, then read the commands at the end closely.

insights.title: Moses wrote
insights.body: "Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys" (33:2). It is one of only a few places where the Torah says Moses himself wrote something down, alongside the battle with Amalek, the covenant at Sinai and the law in Deuteronomy.

insights.title: Forty-two stages
insights.body: Counting Rameses, the list names forty-two places. Jerome wrote a long letter on these "forty-two stations" as stages of the soul's journey, linking them with the forty-two generations of Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. Jewish tradition too has read the journey as a pattern for life's wanderings.

insights.title: Judgments on their gods
insights.body: Israel left Egypt "with a high hand" while Egypt buried its firstborn, and "Yahweh also executed judgments on their gods" (33:3-4). Exodus had promised this before the Passover. The plagues were a contest with Egypt's gods as well as with Pharaoh.

insights.title: Places known from nowhere else
insights.body: Between Hazeroth and Kadesh come about twenty camps, from Rithmah to Ezion Geber (33:18-36), most mentioned nowhere else in Scripture. These are likely the forgotten years of wandering. The list remembers places the story passes over in silence.

insights.title: Ezion Geber
insights.body: Ezion Geber (33:35) lay at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, on the Red Sea. Solomon later built a fleet of ships there for trade. Many of the other places in the list have not been identified with certainty.

insights.title: A precise date for Aaron
insights.body: Aaron's death gets an unusually exact date: the fortieth year after the exodus, the fifth month, the first day (33:38), at the age of 123 (33:39). Jewish tradition marks the first of the month of Av as the anniversary of his death.

insights.title: Destroy their images
insights.body: God commands Israel to drive out the land's inhabitants and destroy their carved stones, metal images and high places (33:52). The target is Canaan's worship, which had just ensnared Israel at Peor. Deuteronomy repeats the command in more detail.

insights.title: Thorns in your sides
insights.body: Those left in the land "will be as pricks in your eyes and as thorns in your sides" (33:55). Joshua repeats the warning, and Judges records it coming true when the tribes failed to drive out the Canaanites.

34.summary: God defines the borders of Canaan, the land the nine and a half tribes west of the Jordan will divide, and names the leaders who will oversee the division.
34.lookfor: Trace the southern, western, northern and eastern borders, and notice which of the named leaders you already know.

names.name: Salt Sea
names.gloss: The Dead Sea.

names.name: Kadesh Barnea
names.gloss: The oasis in the far south where Israel camped for many years.

names.name: brook of Egypt
names.gloss: Probably the Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai, the traditional border with Egypt.

names.name: great sea
names.gloss: The Mediterranean.

names.name: Hamath
names.gloss: A city in Syria; "the entrance of Hamath" marks the far northern border.

names.name: sea of Chinnereth
names.gloss: The Sea of Galilee.

names.name: Caleb
names.gloss: The faithful spy from chapter 13, now the leader chosen for Judah.

skim.advice: Verses 3 to 12 trace the borders by landmarks, and verses 19 to 28 list the tribal leaders. Skim both, noticing the seas and river that frame the land and the familiar names.

insights.title: A map before the battles
insights.body: God draws the land's borders before Israel has crossed the Jordan or fought a single battle west of it (34:2). The map is a promise in the form of a plan. The leaders who will divide it are named in advance too (34:17-29).

insights.title: From the brook of Egypt to Hamath
insights.body: The southern border runs from the Dead Sea to the brook of Egypt (34:3-5), probably the Wadi el-Arish. The northern border reaches "the entrance of Hamath" (34:8), probably Lebo-hamath in Lebanon's Beqaa valley. Israel rarely held so much; Solomon's kingdom is described with the same two limits.

insights.title: The Jordan as the border
insights.body: The eastern border follows the Jordan from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea (34:11-12). So the land just settled by Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh lies outside "the land of Canaan" (34:13-15). The tension surfaces in Joshua 22.

insights.title: Chinnereth
insights.body: The Sea of Galilee is called "the sea of Chinnereth" (34:11). The name is often linked with kinnor, a lyre, because of the lake's shape, though this is uncertain; a town of the same name stood on its shore. In the Gospels it appears as the lake of Gennesaret.

insights.title: Borders in later visions
insights.body: Ezekiel's vision of the restored land uses almost the same boundaries, from Hamath in the north to the brook of Egypt in the south, with the Jordan to the east. God's promise to Abraham in Genesis reaches wider still, to the Euphrates.

insights.title: Caleb still standing
insights.body: Of the ten tribal leaders named here, only one appears in the earlier lists: "Caleb the son of Jephunneh" (34:19). Forty years after he urged Israel to go up, he is chosen to divide the land he spied out. Joshua later records him, at eighty-five, claiming Hebron.

insights.title: Land as gift
insights.body: The land is called "the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance" (34:2). It is never Israel's by conquest alone; it is given and assigned by lot. Leviticus puts it plainly: "the land is mine."

insights.title: Promises with edges
insights.body: God's promise to Israel came with specific borders. How does it help to know the shape of what God has actually promised, rather than what you might wish he had?

35.summary: Israel is to give the Levites forty-eight towns with pastureland, six of them cities of refuge where someone who kills by accident can be safe from the avenger of blood until trial and until the high priest's death.
35.lookfor: Notice how the law distinguishes murder from accidental killing, the part the congregation plays, why the high priest's death matters, and the closing words about blood and the land.

names.name: avenger of blood
names.gloss: The nearest male relative of someone killed, responsible for pursuing the killer.

insights.title: Levite towns and their fields
insights.body: The Levites receive forty-eight towns spread across all the tribes (35:7), each with pastureland measured in thousands of cubits (35:4-5). Later rabbis drew partly on these measurements for the 2,000-cubit limit on Sabbath walking. Acts mentions "a Sabbath day's journey."

insights.title: The six cities named
insights.body: Exodus had promised a place where an accidental killer could flee. Joshua names the six cities: Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron west of the Jordan, and Bezer, Ramoth and Golan to the east (35:14). Deuteronomy adds that the land was to be divided into three parts so that every killer had a refuge within reach.

insights.title: Go'el ha-dam
insights.body: "The avenger of blood" (35:19) is the go'el ha-dam, literally the redeemer of blood. The go'el is the next of kin who protects a family: buying back land, redeeming a relative from slavery, or here pursuing a killer. Job uses the same word when he says, "I know that my Redeemer lives."

insights.title: Intent matters
insights.body: The law weighs the weapon, past hatred and lying in wait (35:16-21) against sudden accidents with no enmity (35:22-23). The congregation, not the avenger, decides which it was (35:24). Jesus later presses further, tracing murder back to anger in the heart.

insights.title: Until the high priest dies
insights.body: The accidental killer must stay in the city of refuge "until the death of the high priest" (35:25, 35:28). Jewish interpreters saw the high priest's death as closing a chapter and bringing release. Christian readers have seen Christ, the great high priest whose death sets the guilty free; Hebrews speaks of believers who have "fled for refuge."

insights.title: No ransom for a murderer
insights.body: A murderer may not pay to escape death (35:31), and the accidental killer may not buy an early return (35:32). Some ancient law codes, like the Hittite laws, allowed compensation for killing. Israel's law treats a human life as beyond price, and requires more than one witness (35:30).

insights.title: Blood pollutes the land
insights.body: "Blood pollutes the land" (35:33), because God dwells in it (35:34). Abel's blood cried from the ground, and God told Noah that whoever sheds human blood answers for it, because humans are made in God's image. Hebrews speaks of Jesus' blood that "speaks better than that of Abel."

insights.title: A city to run to
insights.body: The cities of refuge were for people who had done real harm but without intent. Where can people who carry that kind of guilt find refuge in your community?

36.summary: Leaders of Manasseh worry that Zelophehad's daughters' land could pass to another tribe if they marry outside it, so Moses rules that they must marry within their father's tribe, and the book closes on the plains of Moab.
36.lookfor: Notice the clan's concern, how Moses answers it without overturning the earlier ruling, and what the daughters do.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: Grandson of Manasseh; the clan leaders who raise the case descend from him.

names.name: Machir
names.gloss: Son of Manasseh and father of Gilead.

names.name: Zelophehad
names.gloss: The man of Manasseh who died leaving five daughters and no sons.

names.name: Mahlah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's five daughters.

names.name: Tirzah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's five daughters.

names.name: Hoglah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's five daughters.

names.name: Milcah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's five daughters.

names.name: Noah
names.gloss: One of Zelophehad's five daughters, not Noah of the flood.

insights.title: A follow-up case
insights.body: Chapter 27 solved one problem and raised another. If the daughters married men from other tribes, their land would pass with them, shrinking Manasseh's share (36:3). Israel's law grows as each new question is brought before Moses and God.

insights.title: The jubilee would not help
insights.body: Even the jubilee, when sold land returned to its original family (36:4), would not undo it. Land passed on by inheritance was not a sale, so it would stay with the other tribe for good.

insights.title: Free to choose, within the tribe
insights.body: Moses rules, "Let them be married to whom they think best; only they shall marry into the family of the tribe of their father" (36:6). The women keep their choice, and the tribe keeps its land. They marry their cousins (36:11).

insights.title: Nachalah: inheritance
insights.body: The word nachalah, inheritance, runs through the whole chapter. It means a family's allotted share of the land, held in trust from God rather than owned outright. Naboth later refuses to sell his vineyard to King Ahab because it is "the inheritance of my fathers."

insights.title: The names in a new order
insights.body: In 27:1 the daughters are Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah; here Tirzah moves to second and Noah to last (36:11). Jewish interpreters suggested one list follows their ages and the other a different ranking. Either way, all five are named every time.

insights.title: The land received
insights.body: Joshua records the daughters coming to Eleazar and Joshua to claim their land, and receiving it among their father's brothers. Manasseh's territory was counted in ten parts "because the daughters of Manasseh had an inheritance among his sons."

insights.title: Ending on the plains of Moab
insights.body: Numbers began with a census of fighting men at Sinai and ends with five women securing their family's land in the promised land. The last verse places everything "in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho" (36:13), the setting of Deuteronomy. Leviticus ends at Sinai; Numbers ends at the river.

insights.title: Keeping what was given
insights.body: The book ends with people working out how to keep a gift intact for the next generation. What have you received that you are responsible for passing on?

intro.who: Jewish and Christian tradition receive it as the fourth book of the Torah, given through Moses. Many modern scholars see it as a weaving of priestly material with older stories, poems and lists, reaching its final form during or after the exile.
intro.when: It covers almost forty years, from the second year after the exodus at Sinai to the fortieth year on the plains of Moab across from Jericho (Numbers 1:1; Numbers 33:38). Proposed dates for its writing run from Moses' time to the 6th or 5th century BC, depending on the view.
intro.why: It tells how the generation freed from Egypt refused to trust God and died in the wilderness, while God stayed faithful and brought their children to the edge of the promised land. Its Hebrew name, Bemidbar, means "in the wilderness."
